收藏与公共展览：真题中的反证和信息缺口

用Davies姐妹的原题替换原城市绿化自编判断材料，保留判断训练目标。先读连续片段，再分别判断题干涉及的“童年影响”“艺术顾问态度”“观众反响”，这些不是同一类信息。

Q8＝TRUE：religious upbringing带来social responsibility，随后说明如何使用inheritance，因果关系完整。Q10＝FALSE：Blaker是champion并参与决定，反驳opposed。Q11＝NOT GIVEN：first works…on display in a public gallery仅说明展出事实，不能据此推出very popular with the public。

精读重点是把形容词和关系词保留下来：first≠popular，took advice≠完全被顾问主导，wealthy≠愿意支付任何价格。下一组独立判断Q12、13，并为每题写出原文依据；提交后再查看答案，核对战后改变与当时收藏潮流。

继续做原题片段：The Davies Sisters｜成长背景与收藏起点 · The Davies Sisters｜印象派转向与战时收藏 · The Davies Sisters｜收藏停止与文化遗产

考古器物与糖业：真实摘要的并列顺序和概括

本单元改用真实摘要题，保留“并列结构、词性、信息顺序”的训练。Mapungubwe Q22–26原答案依次是prosperity、whistles、bodies、ancestors、jewellery（或jewelry）。陶器生产规模说明繁荣；ceramic discs已经被题干改为round ceramic objects，下一项才轮到whistles。

Q24的stretched对应原文elongated bodies，不能填旁边的limbs，因为原文说short limbs。Q25的to honour对应as offerings to ancestors；Q26问本地金属制成的物品，所以填jewellery，不填材料copper。每空做完都读回整个句子。

再用Sugar练选词摘要：Q31 H把跨国劳工概括为migrant workers，Q32 E把small farms概括为small-scale cultivation。Q32不能选F outdated methods：traditional并未自动带有“过时”评价。用两组不同原文练同一动作，避免记住一组词后把熟悉感当作会做。

城市噪声与考古：原题中的措施、数据和限定

用Why we need silence替换原社区交通自编信息匹配。Q14问strategies，标准答案C，包含安静公交、道路降噪、航空噪声控制等多个措施。Q15问data indicating the extent，答案B，1 in 5与城市分贝信息说明问题覆盖范围。共同出现noise不能区分两题。

Q17要求“相对安静比完全静音更有益”的比较，答案G：户外花园较完全无声房间让参与者more relaxation and less boredom。只找到“安静有益”的F不够，因为F没有题干要求的两环境对照。

迁移到Mapungubwe：Q16的king’s family对应C中的male relatives，居所是outskirts；B虽然有king，却讲国王本人及顾问在山顶的住所。精读记录“对象、位置、限定”三个格子，避免一个关键词把不同人物合并。

人工智能：用真实作者观点题辨别宣传和判断

本单元使用剑桥21 Artificial Intelligence 的原文和原题，替换原数字学习工具自编段落。开篇的治病、创新等承诺来自sensationalist news和media headlines；作者随后说AI solutionism会jeopardise the value of machine intelligence。媒体印象和作者立场必须分开。

Q36＝NO：题干称Russell建议impractical，原文作者称其sensible and realistic，存在反证。Q37＝NOT GIVEN：Brooks谈创新部署比人们想象更慢，全文没有AI支持者对他的批评，所以不能替作者补一场争论。

Q38＝NO：always taken into account与often overlooked冲突。Q39＝YES：作者要求讨论ethics和distrust来获益并减少危害。答后精读比较while、but、still后语气如何变化；并用真实医疗/司法案例核对作者为何认为AI并非解决一切的方法。

阅读 · 找到判断的证据

学会把题干与原文逐项对应，分清原文明确反对和信息不足。

① 独立作答② 学一处、改一处③ 隔日或新题检查

需要先了解内容时，可以读相关话题背景或常用词与搭配。读过相关提示后，请将本次条件记为“学习后应用”。

01 首次作答02 学习与修订03 参考与核对04 隔日检查原题片段练习

从这份答案开始学

保存首答后，从不确定或答错的题里选一题：先指出原文位置并说出自己的理解，再打开解释，只修清题干与原文之间一个具体关系。关掉解释重新说明判断，保留首答，不以新答案覆盖它。

教学：一次只查清一件事

预计 20—30 分钟，可以另一天完成。

先分清哪里卡住。

  • 尚未找到相关段落：先展示你的候选位置，不把“没找到”直接写成 Not Given。
  • 找到但意思不确定：先用中文说出原句意思，检查否定、比较、时间和指代。
  • 理解原句仍答错：将题干的具体主张与原文比较。原文给出矛盾才是 False；没有足够信息判定则是 Not Given。

本章优先对照第 9、10、11 题：它们涉及来源、态度和公众反应，不能仅因出现同一画家或画廊就判断信息一致。具体解释在参考页，先留下你的理解。

TOPIC 03

科技：工具带来什么，又需要什么条件

科技讨论可以从具体工具怎样改变一件事开始，例如获取资料、观看演出或处理重复任务。线上服务提供了一种渠道，但能连接网络、会使用工具和能够判断信息是不同条件。自动化可以处理部分步骤，责任与判断却需要另外讨论。评价一项技术时，可以比较便利、成本、使用门槛和个人信息的处理方式，也要说明谁受益、谁可能仍需要其他选择。

先分清三个概念

概念它指什么不要混淆
digital access能够使用数字设备、网络及相关服务的条件和机会。拥有设备、能够连接网络与会熟练使用服务并不相同；服务上线也不等于每个人都能使用。
automation让机器或软件按照设定方式完成原本需要人工处理的部分步骤。一项任务自动完成，不等于整个岗位都能被替代；操作、检查和责任可以由不同角色承担。
data privacy个人信息怎样被收集、使用和分享，以及个人对此拥有怎样的选择。隐私关注信息应怎样被使用；安全也关注怎样防止未经许可的访问，二者相关但不能完全互换。

读一段背景英语

Technology changes the way people carry out particular activities. An online service can let a viewer watch a recorded performance without travelling to a theatre. A shared document can allow colleagues in different places to work on the same report. However, having a tool does not settle every question about its use. People still need a suitable device, a connection and enough knowledge to use the service. They may also want to know what personal information it collects. In some situations, an online option adds a useful choice; in others, people may still prefer direct contact or a physical space. A balanced discussion can explain the specific benefit of a tool while considering the conditions needed to use it.
中文帮助理解

科技可以改变完成某项活动的方式：线上服务让人不必前往剧院，也能观看录制的演出；共享文档让不同地点的同事参与同一份报告。不过，有了工具不代表所有使用问题都已经解决。设备、网络和使用知识仍是条件，服务怎样收集个人信息也值得关注。有时线上方式增加了一个有用选择，有时人们仍希望直接接触他人或使用实体空间。讨论可以具体说明工具提供了什么便利，以及这些便利在什么条件下才能实现。

阅读例句

It is technically incorrect to talk about bat 'radar', since they do not use radio waves.

原文区分雷达与蝙蝠的回声定位：讨论科技要分清机制，不能只凭表面相似就当作同一技术。

换到一个具体服务（原创理解练习）

一家社区中心推出网上预约。部分居民没有稳定网络；另一些人有手机却不会操作。系统要求填写身份证号码，并可能受到恶意攻击。请把四件事分别对应 digital access、digital skills、privacy 与 security，再提出一项保留人工帮助的做法。

完成后核对

稳定网络属于 access；会不会使用属于 skills；身份证号码为何收集、谁能看到和保留多久涉及 privacy；防止未授权访问与攻击涉及 security。两者相关，但安全措施完善不表示所有个人信息收集都合理。可保留电话或现场预约，并让工作人员解释必要信息。

原创表达：An online service can make booking easier, provided that users have reliable internet access and know how to use it. Staff should still be available to help people who cannot complete the process online. 用 provided that 写条件，第二句给出需要人工参与的具体环节。

AI 原文支持的是实施条件、攻击风险与人的判断。这里的社区预约和隐私讨论是迁移情境，不是声称原文证明了这些服务的实际效果。

标题匹配：Miles Davis原题中的主旨与干扰项

British Council官方教辅 Miles Davis 的Q14要求给A段选标题。A段开头说十三岁收到小号并开始上课，随后强调这些课塑造了signature sound：其他演奏者喜用vibrato，他被训练成长而直的音色；末句又说这种声音贯穿职业生涯。首句交代年龄和家人，整段落点却是独特演奏风格。

标准答案：Q14＝viii，Davis’ unique style of trumpet playing。干扰项v Childhood and family life只覆盖开头背景，无法概括音色训练、与他人对比及终身延续。主旨应覆盖主要论述，而不只是重复第一句里的年龄或父亲。

再核对Q15＝iii，An education in two parts。B段明确both in the clubs and in the classroom；随后既写退学和对课程的不满，也写后来承认学校在技巧与理论上的价值。因此ii Formal education unhelpful过于绝对，漏掉后半段的肯定。完成原材料的A–F六段后，以“每段讲什么＋作者借此说明什么”各写一句再对答案。

原题完整九个标题为：i A legacy is established；ii Formal education unhelpful；iii An education in two parts；iv Branching out in new directions；v Childhood and family life；vi Change necessary to stay creative；vii Conflicted opinions over Davis’ earlier work；viii Davis’ unique style of trumpet playing；ix Personal and professional struggles。打开完整原文与原题；答后核对官方反馈。

1 Survey the following reading passage. (20 seconds)

MILES DAVIS

Icon and iconoclast¹

A At the age of thirteen, Miles Davis was given his first trumpet, lessons were arranged with a local trumpet player, and a musical odyssey began. These early lessons, paid for and supported by his father, had a profound effect on shaping Davis’ signature sound. Whereas most trumpeters of the era favoured the use of vibrato (a wobbly quiver in pitch inflected in the instrument’s tone), Davis was taught to play with a long, straight tone, a preference his instructor reportedly drilled into the young trumpeter with a rap on the knuckles every time Davis began using vibrato. This clear, distinctive style never left Davis. He continued playing with it for the rest of his career, once remarking, ‘If I can’t get that sound, I can’t play anything.’

B Having graduated from high school in 1944, Davis moved to New York City, where he continued his musical education both in the clubs and in the classroom. His enrolment in the prestigious Julliard School of Music was short-lived, however – he soon dropped out, criticising what he perceived as an over-emphasis on the classical European repertoire and a neglect of jazz. Davis did later acknowledge, however, that this time at the school was invaluable in terms of developing his trumpet-playing technique and giving him a solid grounding in music theory. Much of his early training took place in the form of jam sessions and performances in the clubs of 52nd Street, where he played alongside both up-and-coming and established members of the jazz pantheon such as Coleman Hawkins, Eddie ‘Lockjaw’ Davis, and Thelonious Monk.

C In the late 1940s, Davis collaborated with nine other instrumentalists, including a French horn and a tuba player, to produce The Birth of Cool, an album now renowned for the inchoate sounds of what would later become known as ‘cool’ jazz. In contrast to popular jazz styles of the day, which featured rapid, rollicking beats, shrieking vocals, and short, sharp horn blasts, Davis’ album was the forerunner of a different kind of sound – thin, light horn-playing, hushed drums and a more restrained, formal arrangement. Although it received little acclaim at the time (the liner notes to one of Davis’ later recordings call it a ‘spectacular failure’), in hindsight The Birth of Cool has become recognised as a pivotal moment in jazz history, cementing – alongside his 1958 recording, Kind of Blue – Davis’ legacy as one of the most innovative musicians of his era.

D Though Davis’ trumpet playing may have sounded effortless and breezy, this ease rarely carried over into the rest of his life. The early 1950s, in particular, were a time of great personal turmoil. After returning from a stint in Paris, Davis suffered from prolonged depression, which he attributed to the unravelling of a number of relationships, including his romance with a French actress and some musical partnerships that ruptured as a result of creative disputes. Davis was also frustrated by his perception that he had been overlooked by the music critics, who were hailing the success of his collaborators and descendants in the ‘cool’ tradition, such as Gerry Mulligan and Dave Brubeck, but who afforded him little credit for introducing the cool sound in the first place.

E In the latter decades of his career, Davis broke out of exclusive jazz settings and began to diversify his output across a range of musical styles. In the 1960s, he was influenced by early funk performers such as Sly and the Family Stone, which then expanded into the jazz-rock fusion genre – of which he was a frontrunner – in the 1970s. Electronic recording effects and electric instruments were incorporated into his sound. By the 1980s, Davis was pushing the boundaries further, covering pop anthems such as Cyndi Lauper’s Time After Time and Michael Jackson’s Human Nature, dabbling in hip hop, and even appearing in some movies.

F Not everyone was supportive of Davis’ change of tune. Compared to the recordings of his early career, universally applauded as linchpins of the jazz oeuvre, trumpeter Wynston Marsalis derided his fusion work as being ‘not true jazz’, and pianist Bill Evans denounced the ‘corrupting influence’ of record companies, noting that rock and pop ‘draw wider audiences’. In the face of this criticism Davis remained defiant, commenting that his earlier recordings were part of a moment in time that he had no ‘feel’ for any more. He firmly believed that remaining stylistically inert would have hampered his ability to develop new ways of producing music. From this perspective, Davis’ continual revamping of genre was not merely a rebellion, but an evolution, a necessary path that allowed him to release his full musical potential.

¹ An iconoclast is somebody who challenges traditional beliefs or customs
